**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Recommendation on our compute capacity decision for the next two quarters

We've reached the point where our inference cluster is running hot. Peak-hour GPU utilisation sits above 85%, queue times during business hours have crept from seconds to minutes, and two teams have told us they're delaying experiments because they can't get reliable access to hardware. The instinctive response — buy more GPUs — deserves scrutiny before we commit, because the alternative path (improving utilisation of what we own) is cheaper, faster, and far easier to undo if we're wrong.

Let me start with cost, since it frames everything else. A modest hardware expansion — say, four additional accelerators plus the networking, power, and cooling changes that come with them — would run well into six figures once you include the operational overhead we tend to underestimate: rack space, failover capacity, and the engineering time to integrate and monitor new machines. Utilisation work, by contrast, is mostly engineering time we already control. Batching improvements, better request scheduling, quantising two of our heavier models, and moving batch workloads to off-peak windows could plausibly lift effective utilisation from the mid-eighties to the low nineties. That doesn't sound dramatic, but at our scale it recovers roughly the equivalent of one to two GPUs' worth of capacity — for a fraction of the purchase price.

Latency is the strongest argument on the hardware side, and I want to be honest about it. Utilisation gains are not free. Tighter batching and more aggressive scheduling reduce idle capacity but can add milliseconds of queuing per request, and quantisation carries a small accuracy cost that we'd need to validate carefully. If our product requirements demand strict tail latencies at peak, there's a limit to how hard we can squeeze the existing fleet before user experience suffers. My view is that we haven't hit that limit yet — our p99 latency is still comfortably within our SLO for most endpoints — but we're closer to it than we were six months ago, and that trajectory matters.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware gives us headroom for failover and maintenance windows, which is genuinely valuable; right now a single node failure during peak hours degrades service in a way that's visible to users. But utilisation improvements can also serve reliability: right-sizing workloads, eliminating the memory pressure that causes occasional OOM restarts, and building proper load-shedding all make the current fleet more resilient without adding physical complexity. Buying hardware to solve a reliability problem we could fix in software would be the expensive way out.

The opportunity cost question is the one I keep returning to. Every dollar and every engineer-week spent on procurement is a dollar and a week not spent on the product work that actually differentiates us. Hardware purchases also lock us in: accelerator generations turn over quickly, resale values are poor, and a purchase made for today's workload profile may be poorly matched to whatever we're building in eighteen months. Utilisation work, by contrast, builds durable organisational capability. Learning to schedule, batch, and right-size well pays off regardless of what hardware we eventually own — and if we do buy later, we'll buy less of it because we'll know our true demand profile instead of our current inefficiency.

That points to reversibility as the deciding factor. Utilisation improvements are largely reversible and incremental; if a scheduling change hurts latency, we roll it back in an afternoon. Hardware is not reversible in any practical sense. Given genuine uncertainty about where our workload is heading — our traffic mix has shifted twice this year already — I'd rather make the reversible bet first and keep the option to buy open.

So my recommendation is this: commit the next quarter to a focused utilisation effort with explicit targets — p99 latency held within SLO, effective utilisation above 90%, and queue times back under ten seconds at peak. We should also pre-approve a hardware purchase contingent on those targets being missed, so we're not stuck re-litigating if the software path falls short. That gives us a fast, cheap attempt at solving the problem with a credible, pre-committed fallback.

The honest caveat is that we don't fully understand our demand curve. If growth accelerates beyond current forecasts, utilisation work will buy us time, not a solution — and we should treat this memo as the first step in a decision we'll revisit, not the last word on it.

Happy to discuss at Thursday's planning session.
